items.prompt: Order the high-level steps for counting connected components in an undirected graph whose vertex set is 0 through n−1.

elements.text: Initialize all vertices as unseen and set count to zero.
Scan vertices in the declared vertex set.
When the current vertex is unseen, increment count.
From that vertex, mark its entire reachable region seen with BFS or DFS.

feedback.reason: The count advances exactly when the outer scan finds a vertex not covered by any earlier traversal.

blocks.text: One unseen root corresponds to one new component

items: Mark every declared vertex unseen and initialize count = 0.
When vertex u is unseen, increment count once.
Run BFS or DFS from u and mark its entire reachable region before the scan continues.

blocks.text: After the inner traversal, every vertex connected to u is seen and will be skipped. A later unseen vertex cannot belong to u's component, because the traversal would otherwise have reached it, so it proves exactly one new maximal connected region.

blocks.title: Counting invariant
blocks.text: Increment once per unseen outer-loop root, never per vertex, edge, enqueue, or dequeue.

items.prompt: An undirected graph declares vertices {0,1,2,3,4,5}. Its edges are {0—1, 1—2, 3—4}; vertex 5 is isolated. How many connected components does it have?

feedback.reason: The components are {0,1,2}, {3,4}, and the isolated singleton {5}.

blocks.text: Partition the complete declared vertex set

items: Edges 0—1 and 1—2 connect {0,1,2} into one maximal set.
Vertex 5 is reachable from itself by a zero-edge path and forms singleton component {5}.

blocks.text: The three components are therefore {0,1,2}, {3,4}, and {5}. Answer 2 drops the isolate; answer 4 splits vertices already joined by paths; answer 6 ignores that connected vertices share one component.

blocks.title: Isolate rule
blocks.text: Every declared isolated vertex is a one-vertex connected component.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two: This counts only edge-containing groups and incorrectly drops the isolated declared vertex.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.four: Vertices 0, 1, and 2 are mutually connected through paths and form one component, not separate components.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.six: A component is a maximal path-connected set; an edge can join several vertices into one component.

items.prompt: A directed graph contains edges A → B and C → B. The task asks for strongly connected components. Is the ordinary undirected component-counting outer loop with one BFS/DFS sufficient?

options.text: Yes; ignore directions and count one weak component.
No; one-way reachability is not mutual reachability, so an SCC algorithm with directed structure is required.
Yes; BFS is always faster than DFS and therefore discovers strong components correctly.
Yes, provided the graph uses an adjacency matrix.

feedback.reason: Strong connectivity requires paths in both directions, which one ordinary traversal from a root does not certify.

blocks.text: One-way reachability is not strong connectivity

items: A can reach B, but B cannot return to A.
C can reach B, but B cannot return to C.
Thus {A}, {B}, and {C} are three separate strongly connected components.

blocks.text: An ordinary traversal from A can mark both A and B and incorrectly treat one-way reachability as a component. Ignoring direction instead computes one weak component {A,B,C}. SCC algorithms require directed invariants such as finish order with a reversed graph or low-link structure.

blocks.title: Relation boundary
blocks.text: The simple outer-loop traversal counts undirected components, not directed strongly connected components.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_direction: That computes weak connectivity and changes the requested strong-connectivity relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_sufficient: Traversal order cannot turn one-way paths into mutual reachability or supply the missing SCC invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_sufficient: Representation does not change the definition of strong connectivity.

items.prompt: While counting undirected components, when should the component counter be incremented?

options.text: Every time a vertex is enqueued, because every queue entry represents a component.
For each edge that connects two previously unseen vertices.
Whenever a duplicate vertex is dequeued after late visited marking.
Once, immediately before starting a traversal from an unseen outer-loop vertex.

feedback.reason: The unseen outer-loop root is the one event that proves a new maximal reachable region begins.

blocks.text: Count the event that proves a new region

An unseen outer-loop vertex was not reached by any earlier component traversal. It therefore lies in a different maximal connected region, so increment immediately before launching the BFS or DFS that consumes that region.

blocks.title: Local work is not a component boundary
blocks.text: A component may enqueue many vertices, contain many edges or cycles, or contain no edges at all. Duplicate frontier entries are implementation work, not new regions.

blocks.title: Counter placement
blocks.text: Increment once at each unseen outer-loop root, then mark its whole component.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.on_every_enqueue: Queue entries represent vertices inside one component; incrementing there counts traversal work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.on_every_edge: A component may contain many edges, cycles, or no edges; edge count is not component count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.on_dequeue_duplicate: Duplicate frontier entries are an implementation defect or guarded condition, not evidence of another component.

items.prompt: For a static undirected graph stored as adjacency lists, the only output is the number of connected components. Which traversal choice is correct?

options.text: Only recursive DFS without visited state, because each component becomes a tree.
Only BFS, because breadth order defines components and is always faster.
Either cycle-safe BFS or cycle-safe DFS; both partition the graph into the same reachable regions in O(V + E).
Either traversal works only after converting the graph to an adjacency matrix.

feedback.reason: Component identity depends on reachability closure, which both BFS and DFS compute.

blocks.text: Component identity is independent of traversal order

items: BFS exhausts one root's reachable set in breadth layers.
DFS exhausts the same reachable set by following depth branches.
Across the outer scan, each vertex is discovered once and adjacency-list scans total O(E), so either choice costs O(V + E).

blocks.text: Use iterative DFS when call depth is unsafe or BFS when another output needs layers. Neither choice removes the visited requirement in a cyclic component, and neither requires conversion to a matrix.

blocks.title: Choice rule
blocks.text: For component count alone, any complete cycle-safe BFS or DFS is correct.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_only: Components depend on reachability, not layer order; DFS reaches the same region under the same graph contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_no_visited: The input component may contain cycles; the traversal tree does not eliminate non-tree edges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_required: Adjacency lists already support complete neighbor expansion and preserve O(V + E) cost.

items.prompt: An edge list for n vertices is converted to adjacency lists, but the implementation creates a list entry only when a vertex appears in an edge. What component-counting failure can result?

options.text: Every edge-containing component is merged into one because lists cannot represent separation.
Isolated declared vertices are absent from the outer scan and their singleton components are not counted.
The count remains correct; only BFS becomes slower than DFS.
Marking visited on dequeue restores the missing singleton vertices.

feedback.reason: Component counting ranges over vertices, so representation must preserve the complete declared vertex set.

blocks.text: Build vertices from n, not from edge endpoints

items: Create n empty adjacency collections for vertices 0 through n−1.
Insert each edge into the appropriate endpoint collections.
Scan all n entries, including collections that remain empty.
Each empty unseen entry starts and completes a singleton component.

blocks.text: Creating entries only for edge endpoints deletes isolated vertices from the represented graph and can undercount by one for every omitted isolate. BFS versus DFS and visited timing cannot discover a state absent from the vertex set.

blocks.title: Representation invariant
blocks.text: The declared vertex set owns outer-loop coverage; edges only populate adjacency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.merges_components: Adjacency lists can represent disconnected graphs; the defect is omission of vertices with no edges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_slower_only: The missing vertices change the represented graph and therefore the count, independent of traversal order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.late_mark_fix: Visited timing cannot discover a vertex that was omitted from the declared scan and representation.

items.prompt: A binary grid counts islands using orthogonal adjacency. The same occupied cells form two islands under 4-direction movement but one island when diagonal movement is also legal. What explains the change?

options.text: Eight-direction BFS is faster, so it is allowed to merge components.
Marking on dequeue merges diagonal cells even when diagonals are forbidden.
A grid is always one tree, and the component difference is only output formatting.
The vertex set is the same, but the legal-move rule changes the graph's edges and therefore its connected components.

feedback.reason: Components are defined relative to the graph's edge relation, and diagonal moves add edges.

blocks.text: Changing legal moves changes the graph

For example, occupied cells (0,0) and (1,1) share only a corner. Under four-direction movement there is no edge between them, so they are two components. Under eight-direction movement the diagonal move adds an edge, so they become one component.

The outer scan and BFS or DFS algorithm are unchanged; they are operating on different edge relations. Speed, visited timing, and output formatting cannot legally merge vertices when the movement contract forbids the connecting edge.

blocks.title: Modeling rule
blocks.text: Connected components are defined by both the vertex set and the exact legal-edge relation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_speed: Algorithm speed cannot change the mathematical connectivity relation; the new diagonal edges do.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_timing: Visited timing affects scheduling, not which transitions are legal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_rule: Grid graphs can contain cycles and disconnected regions; adjacency rules define their topology.

items.prompt: A component counter receives n declared vertices and an edge list that mentions only some of them. What initialization is required?

options.text: Create adjacency and visited entries for every declared vertex, including isolated vertices.
Create entries only for vertices that occur in an edge because isolated vertices cannot form components.
Start from vertex 0 and count only what it reaches.
Sort the edge list and infer isolated vertices from gaps without scanning the vertex set.

feedback.reason: The declared vertex set, not only the edge list, defines the components being counted.

blocks.text: An isolated vertex is a component of size one. The outer scan must visit every identifier 0 through n-1 and start a traversal when it is unvisited. Omitting adjacency entries can silently drop isolated vertices and undercount the answer.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.edge_vertices_only: A vertex with no edges still forms a singleton component.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_start: One traversal covers only one connected region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_edges: Edge gaps require a complete vertex-domain scan and sorting alone does not traverse components.

items.prompt: An undirected graph contains the same edge {u,v} twice. How should a correct component count treat the duplicate?

options.text: It does not create another component; duplicate adjacency may be traversed once or tolerated with visited checks.
Increment the component count for every duplicate edge.
Treat the second occurrence as a new copy of u and v.
Any duplicate edge makes component counting undefined.

feedback.reason: Connected components depend on reachability, and repeating an existing connection does not change reachability.

blocks.text: The adjacency list can contain duplicate neighbor entries without changing the visited set. Marking vertices prevents repeated traversal from changing the count. A simple-graph input may reject duplicates, but they are not new vertices or components by themselves.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.count_edge_as_component: Components are vertex sets, not edge counts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.split_vertices: An edge occurrence does not create new vertex identities.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reject_graph: The representation may permit multiedges; reachability remains well-defined.

items.prompt: A task asks for weakly connected components of a directed graph. Which preprocessing interpretation is required?

options.text: Treat each directed edge as an undirected connection for the weak-component traversal.
Traverse outgoing edges only and call each reachability region a strongly connected component.
Use only incoming edges because weak connectivity is defined by predecessors.
Topologically sort first; every directed graph has a topological order for this count.

feedback.reason: Weak connectivity ignores edge orientation, while strongly connected components require mutual directed reachability and a different algorithmic contract.

blocks.text: For each directed edge u→v, weak connectivity links u and v regardless of direction. The outer traversal then counts components in that undirected interpretation. Following outgoing edges only computes source reachability, not weak components or SCCs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.outgoing_only_scc: A one-way connection can join a weak component without making its endpoints mutually reachable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.incoming_only: Weak connectivity uses both endpoints symmetrically.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.topological_order: Cycles may exist, and topological sorting is not the component-counting contract.

items.prompt: In a connected-components traversal, what event starts a new component count?

options.text: An outer-loop vertex that is still unvisited becomes a new traversal seed.
Every edge increments the component count.
Every queue pop creates another component.
The highest-degree vertex always starts the next component.

feedback.reason: One traversal exhausts exactly one reachable component; an unvisited outer-loop vertex proves another remains.

blocks.text: Mark the seed before exploring. All vertices reached from it share one component count, and the outer loop advances only to a new unvisited region.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.every_edge: Many edges can belong to one component.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_empty: A queue becomes empty after each component, but the next component is counted at its new seed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.highest_degree: Degree order is not required for correctness.

items.prompt: How does an isolated vertex affect the number of connected components in an undirected graph?

options.text: It forms a component of size one.
It is ignored because components require at least one edge.
It merges every component into one.
It always contributes two components because it has degree zero.

feedback.reason: Connectivity includes the zero-edge path from a vertex to itself.

blocks.text: An outer-loop traversal visits the isolated vertex, marks it, and finishes immediately; that seed still increments the component count once.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignored: A vertex is a valid connected component even without edges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_graph: No edge connects it to other components.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_components: Degree zero describes isolation, not two separate vertices.

items.prompt: In a grid component count, what must the outer scan do after finishing one flood fill?

options.text: Continue scanning for another traversable cell that is not yet visited.
Stop because one flood fill always covers the whole grid.
Clear visited cells before searching for the next component.
Sort all remaining cells before the next fill.

feedback.reason: A flood fill covers one connected region; disconnected traversable regions still require new seeds.

blocks.text: Visited state must persist across fills. Resetting it would revisit earlier regions and destroy the component partition.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stop_first: The grid may contain several disconnected regions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reset_visited: Persistent visited state is what prevents duplicate component counts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_cells: Grid adjacency, not cell order, defines connectivity.

items.prompt: For counting undirected connected components, what correctness property is shared by DFS and BFS?

options.text: Either traversal visits exactly the vertices reachable from each component seed.
They must visit vertices in the same order.
Both guarantee shortest paths in every graph.
They always use identical auxiliary memory.

feedback.reason: Component counting needs reachability coverage, not a particular frontier order.

blocks.text: DFS uses a stack or recursion and BFS uses a queue, but both mark each reached vertex and exhaust one connected region before the next seed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_order: Frontier discipline produces different visit orders.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_shortest_path: DFS does not generally produce shortest paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_memory: Recursion, explicit stacks, and queues can have different peak shapes.

items.prompt: When counting components with BFS, why is marking a vertex visited at enqueue time preferred?

options.text: It prevents the same vertex from entering the queue through multiple neighbors.
It guarantees every vertex is processed before any duplicate can appear.
It marks all vertices only after the component is complete.
It marks a vertex only when the outer loop reaches it.

feedback.reason: Discovery-time marking makes queue membership unique.

blocks.text: A vertex can have several already-discovered neighbors. Mark it when enqueued so each vertex contributes at most one queue entry and the traversal remains linear.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_dequeue: Late marking can enqueue duplicates before the first copy is removed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_component_end: Waiting until the component ends loses the guard during traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_outer_scan: The outer scan finds seeds but does not cover neighbor discovery.

items.prompt: A graph declares vertices 0 through 4, but only edges 0-1 and 1-2. What must a correct component count include?

options.text: Two components: {0,1,2} and {3,4}.
Three components: the connected group plus each isolated vertex.
One component because all declared vertices share the same graph object.
Zero because the graph has no edge touching every vertex.

feedback.reason: Declared isolated vertices are singleton components.

blocks.text: Vertices 3 and 4 have no edges, but each is reachable from itself and from no other vertex. The total is one three-vertex component plus two singleton components.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two: There are two isolated vertices, not one combined component.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one: A graph container does not create connectivity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Component counting includes valid zero-degree vertices.

items.prompt: What changes when the same outer-loop traversal is used to count components in a directed graph?

options.text: Following outgoing edges counts weak connectivity unless reverse edges are also considered.
The answer is always identical to the undirected graph.
The component count equals the number of directed edges.
Directed edges cannot be traversed with BFS or DFS.

feedback.reason: Direction changes the reachability relation used by the traversal.

blocks.text: A traversal that follows outgoing edges computes reachability under direction. Weak components require treating edges as undirected, while strongly connected components need a dedicated algorithm and definition.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_always: Directed reachability can differ from undirected connectivity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.edge_count: Edges do not directly determine component count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_impossible: BFS and DFS can follow outgoing directed edges.

items.prompt: A component-counting loop resets visited to false before each new outer-loop seed. What is the consequence?

options.text: Previously visited regions can be traversed again and the count can be inflated.
The reset makes the traversal asymptotically faster.
Resetting merges all components into one.
Visited state is irrelevant after a seed is chosen.

feedback.reason: Visited state must persist across all component searches.

blocks.text: After a reset, vertices from earlier components look unseen and can start duplicate traversals. The outer loop must reuse one visited structure for the whole graph.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.faster: Repeated work can increase time rather than reduce it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.merge: Resetting separates work incorrectly; it does not add edges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_effect: Visited state is the guard that prevents duplicate component counts.
